item.title: Akiyoshidai
item.description:
About

From https://tech-diving.jp/akiyoshidai

What is Akiyoshidai? Akiyoshidai is Japan’s largest karst plateau , located in the central and eastern parts of Mine City, Yamaguchi Prefecture. Its limestone distribution covers approximately 93 km², a scale unparalleled anywhere else in Japan.

More than 400 limestone caves have been identified in Akiyoshidai, including Akiyoshido Cave , one of Japan’s three largest limestone caves and a designated special natural monument.

Akiyoshidai is divided into two plateaus, Higashidai and Nishidai, by the Higashikawa River . Higashidai (Akiyoshidai in the narrow sense) was designated a national park (Akiyoshidai National Park) in 1955 and a special natural monument in 1964. In addition, individual caves are registered as natural monuments, and meticulous care is taken in their maintenance and management.

item.title: Algeria
item.description:
About

Algeria features a diverse landscape that includes mountain ranges, vast deserts, and karstic plateaus, making it highly relevant from a speleological and geological perspective.

🪨 Limestone Karst in Algeria

Yes, Algeria has significant limestone karst formations, especially in the northern and northeastern regions of the country. These include:

  • Djurdjura Mountains (part of the Tell Atlas): This region has well-developed karst plateaus with numerous caves and sinkholes, formed in Jurassic and Cretaceous limestones.
  • **Constantine and Setif regions**: Known for complex karst systems and underground hydrology.
  • Tassili n’Ajjer (southeastern Algeria - DO NOT TRAVEL): While primarily known for its sandstone formations and prehistoric rock art, some karst-like erosion features occur in isolated carbonate outcrops.

🕳️ Caves in Algeria

Algeria has extensive cave systems, many of which are of speleological, ecological, or archaeological interest. Notable caves include:

item.title: Allendale - 5L11
item.description:
From CaveDB

Known as the ‘hole in the middle of the road’, Allendale is one the of the first CDAA Cave Rated sites that divers have access in the earlier steps of their cave training. The cave consists of a main straight tunnel on a 45 degrees slope reaching 26m depth at the bottom and a total 60m length (from surface to deepest part). A small surface lake can host divers comfortably with water level usually at below waist level. The Northwest corner of the lake will grant access to the cave’s main tunnel which is reasonably large until you reach 12m depth after a 25m swim. Attentive divers will notice on their right hand side that some sort of collapse happened there. The main tunnel branches East at the 12 m restriction, and one can navigate through a narrow passage until hitting a full stop after a roughly 15 metres swim. Back to the main tunnel and once cleared the 12m depth mark, divers will face a large room spanning 30m in length (to the deepest part of the cave) and 20m in width. Behind the black silt pile on the Northwest corner a fissure on the rock has been object of many divers work. She doesn’t go, yet…

item.title: Allendale East Cave – Soggy Wombats
item.description:
Allendale East Cave

Introduction

Known as the hole in the middle of the road or just ‘the Dale’, Allendale East Cave is a very popular site among the CDAA Cave rated divers in the Mount Gambier region. As it presents itself as a non-complex cave to dive in, the Soggy Wombats Team has been training, developing skills and accumulating experience in this cave since 2019. Although geographically far from the most developed cave systems in the region, ‘the Dale’ has a small ‘tunnel’ at it’s deepest end that has been in most of Australian’s Cave Divers dreams to break into something big. There hasn’t been any breakthrough in this cave in the last 20 years or so, but with the advances in exploration techniques, we might be surprised with what the future will tell us.

item.title: Armenia
item.description:
About

Area of Interest: Vayots Dzor, Syunik, Tavush Moderate to High Cave Potential

  • Large parts of Armenia’s landscape are limestone and dolomite, particularly in the Vayots Dzor, Syunik, and Tavush provinces.
  • Features rugged terrain with karst valleys, dolines, and numerous caves, many of which are still actively being mapped by local and European caving groups.

Known Caves

  • Mozrov Cave, Magili Cave, and Arjeri Cave are significant dry caves.
  • Armenia is known for deep fissure systems and vertical caves — some of which contain seasonal sumps or intermittent water pools.

Cave Diving Status

  • No published records of cave diving expeditions.
  • Numerous karst springs, resurgences, and hydrothermal systems may offer dive potential, particularly at mid-altitudes where the water table is accessible.

Exploration Potential

  • High chance of discovering new phreatic or resurgence caves.
  • Requires satellite scouting and geological mapping to identify high-potential karst spring zones.
  • Local geology and hydrology suggest first-descent opportunities, especially during spring melt (April–June).

item.title: Article - Corra-Lynn
item.description: When I tell people I’ve just met that I’m a cave diver with claustrophobia, I always get a few confused looks followed by an inevitable round of questions along the lines of “Oh, so how do you stop the panic then?”. But when I mention my claustrophobia to people who know me and the kind of cave diving I do, the reaction is generally more like “You are very clearly broken, Josh - what is wrong with your brain?”.

item.title: Article - Iddlebiddy Cave - Soggy Wombats - DRAFT
item.description:
Introduction

First discovered sometime in the early 1980’s by an enthusiastic band of unqualified local divers, Iddlebiddy Cave was named as a tongue-in-cheek nod to far larger Cocklebiddy Cave on the Nullarbor Plains which is resembles in structure if not in size. The location of Iddlebiddy Cave remained a closely guarded secret for several years, until it was first formally surveyed on 26 November 1988 by Tony Hambling, Frank Homewood and John McCormick on behalf of the Cave Divers Association of Australia.

item.title: Bakers Cave - 5L285
item.description:
From CaveDB

🗺️ Site Overview

The site features a vertical solution tube approximately 1 meter in diameter, descending around 16 meters to reach the water. Divers can swim to a clean rock in waist-deep water, which serves as a stable platform for donning or doffing dive gear.

The dive itself includes a spacious underwater main chamber that connects to a tunnel reaching a maximum depth of 33 meters.

item.title: Bulgaria
item.description:
About

Rhodope Mountains

  • Why: Part of the same karst belt as the Balkans; caves like Duhlata are among the longest in Eastern Europe.
  • Status: Extensive dry cave exploration but fewer cave diving ventures than Western Europe.
  • Potential: High-value survey targets with minimal diving records.
  • Best Season: June to September.

item.description:
About

Mandara Mountains Karst (CLOSE TO NIGERIA - DO NOT TRAVEL)

  • Why: Unique tropical karst topography near the Nigerian border with surface limestone exposures.
  • Status: Negligible caving or diving work; area is geologically promising.
  • Potential: Spring and cave pool diving in little-documented karst regions.
  • Best Season: December to February.

item.title: Cavetone Park Estate Cave - 5L179

Caveton Park Estate Cave - a49bb2e5

2022DEC: MW & BC found sign reading “L940”, dropped down 6m solution tube, identified cave as L179 (Caveton Park Estate Cave). NW corner chokes to “Block” (dive beyond), SE corner chokes to soft soil that needs digging

Upcoming

  • May - Stan Flavel- May probably the 3rd weekend, date TBA possibly 15th May- going to the Flinders, suitable for any level of caver- will be investigating some bat caves and a bit of surface stuff. Weather dependent of course! (tadarida7@gmail.com)
  • Matt Smith - keen to organise some SRT training in Adelaide so new members can get into Sellicks Caves. Also keen for a newbie trip to Naracoorte sometime- contact Matt if you would like to help organise a trip. (hellboy1975@gmail.com)
  • Grant Gartrell - will be running a trip to Centenary Cave, Myponga at Myponga sometime in the next few months- will also be weather dependent. (blueberrypatch@bigpond.com)

item.title: Cocklebiddy Cave - 6N48
item.description:
From ASF

About

Cocklebiddy Cave is over 6.5km long and is the longest single underwater passage in Australia. The entrance is in a degraded doline 120m long and a steep talus slope beneath overhang at the North end leads to large chamber 360 x 45 x 30m high with 180m long lake. The lake contains “mud islands”.

It is possible to snorkel the lake to look down at the first sump, the water can be muddy after rain.

About

Katanga (Shaba) Plateau

  • Why: Massive, remote karst regions in southern DRC near the Zambian border.
  • Status: Very limited cave exploration; almost no diving records.
  • Potential: First expeditions into flooded karst systems—logistically challenging but potentially world-class.
  • Best Season: May to August.

item.description:
From CaveDB

Ewens Ponds 3 - 6c098cc4

No-Mount entry with significant flow pushing out of cave. Dive currently terminates at 19m in down sloping flattener with extreme flow at pinch point

Ewens Ponds 4 - e35d294b

2021-Feb: MW swam down from Ewen’s 3rd pond. Simple dead end in swamp, no apparent leads or springs.

item.title: Fossil Cave - 5L81
item.description:
From CaveDB

Fossil cave is named for the fossils found there so care must be taken not to disturb these. It is a doline collapse that has east and west dives. The west side is a shortish cave level dive that has many nooks and cranies to explore. The west is bigger and rated cave for the most part but there is a restriction at 13m that you must be cave rated to pass and enters the tank cave system.

item.title: Goa Lalauwi
item.description:
Other Descriptions

About

From Anita: - This is a cave that deserves a special mention. A 600m submerged tunnel leads into the heart of the cave. So far around 3km of tunnels have been explored, yet the cave keeps on going. Goa Lalauwi keeps a few secrets up its sleeve as it wants you to come back for more. On my first dive we swam through big tunnels with white limestone, sections of fractured rock and large areas of stalagmites in crystal clear blue water. To get to the water you walk over 100 steps down a dry chamber which means the cave it self is never exposed to any sunlight. It’s pitch black. This means you are reliant on your torch as soon as you step into the cave. It is quite slippery at the entrance lake and you need to take care not to slip and fall. Then you kit up inside the lake aided by your torch light before the descent towards the first tunnel. The second dive in this beauty was far more complex from a navigational perspective with lots of directional decisions and several jumps that lead to a section with little white humps in the form of witches’ hats. According to our guide, these formations are considered quite rare and, unlike the other speleothems in the caves, form under water. While I have spent several hours in this cave, I will be back for more.

item.title: Gua La Pahia
item.description:
Other Descriptions

To Do

Diving Dry Photogrammetry

About

“The House Cave” for Kadena Glamping Muna

  • From Anita:
    • “In the backyard of where we stayed lies Goa La Pahia, the hidden cave, with an unassuming small rock entrance surrounded by vegetation. As you descend, it slowly unveils its secrets. Calcite crystal formations decorate the ceiling. which tum into whole sections covered in crystal straws. As you swim further along the cave it reveals more and more of its unique formations. Small but impressive, it has a special place in my heart. The first underwater crystal cave that I have ever seen was a dream come true. The sheer beauty, uniqueness and the masses of speleothems took a while to sink in. I was on such a high, but at the same time I was so calm and close to a meditative state as I took in the surroundings with awe and wonder. This was my introduction to cave diving in Muna Island. What a phenomenal start that made me curious for what lay in store for the coming days.”

Logged Dives

  • 2025-08-04 - Gua La Pahia

item.description:

You need a permit issued by ForestrySA

item.title: Iceland
item.description:
Iceland is listed under Europe in Cave Regions.

Cave Regions

  • No local cave regions listed yet.

Caves & Dive Sites

  • See the linked cave regions above.

Backlinks

  • Cave Regions
  • Diving

Existing Notes

About

Go June to September? (Summer)

  • Calmest Weather & Longest Days:
    Iceland experiences milder weather, longer daylight hours (up to 24 hours near the solstice), and calmer surface conditions during summer. This makes logistics easier and safer, particularly when accessing remote dive sites.
  • Better Accessibility:
    Many of Iceland’s cave dive sites are in remote highland regions or near lava fields — during winter and spring, snow and ice can make these areas impassable. Roads are generally fully open by mid-June and remain accessible until early autumn.
  • Consistent Water Temperatures:
    Iceland’s groundwater-fed cave systems (like those at Silfra and Davíðsgjá) maintain constant temperatures year-round (~2–4°C), so water temps aren’t your limiting factor — surface conditions and access are.
  1. Silfra Fissure (Þingvellir National Park)
    • While not a cave in the traditional sense, Silfra offers crystal-clear visibility (~100m) in a tectonic fissure between the North American and Eurasian plates.
    • Accessible year-round, but summer offers the best overall experience due to comfort during gear changes and travel ease.
  2. Davíðsgjá
    • A darker, slightly deeper alternative to Silfra with limited overhead sections.
    • Best dived in summer for similar reasons — ease of access and surface comfort.
  3. Litlaá Lava Tube Cave Systems (near Lake Mývatn)
    • Actual underwater lava tube systems, rare and remote.
    • These are less developed for tourism and require expedition-level planning.
    • Only realistically accessible between July and early September.

Avoid October to May

item.title: Iddlebiddy Cave - 5L250
item.description:
From CaveDB

Iddlebiddy Cave is a 250m single passage-way, which runs from the entrance chamber and ends in a small, silty room containing an array of largely-formed clay deposits.

Divers must take care when venturing into this cave, as the soft walls and delicate features located in the long passage make the water susceptible to clouding. Divers are encouraged to take their time passing through the passage, to enjoy the many cave features and avoid causing finning or physical damage.

item.title: Jam Cave - 5L301
item.description:
From CaveDB

BC visited 04/23: 70 cm hole descending straight down. Need ropes to enter exit, ideally an ascender as it is a hard climb out. Opens in 5m cavern area with big mound in the center that looks like accumulation or someone trying to fill it. Area at the bottom of the pile has fresh water in it. Digging is hard and there will be a lot of material to remove for any hope of progressing.

item.title: Kenya
item.description:
About

Kenya features both limestone karst landscapes and opportunities for cave diving, particularly along its coastal regions.

🪨 Limestone Karst in Kenya

Kenya’s coastal areas, notably around Vipingo in Kilifi County, are characterized by coralline limestone formations that have undergone karstification. These processes have led to the development of features such as caves, sinkholes, and underground voids. For instance, studies at the Vipingo Coral Limestone Quarry have documented various karst features and associated geohazards, including cavities and fissures in the rock mass. (ej-geo.org)

item.title: Kilbsy's Sinkhole - 5L46
item.description:
From CaveDB

Kilsby Sinkhole is a naturally occurring karst sinkhole located on private property 10 kilometres south-west of Mount Gambier in South Australia. The sinkhole is renowned worldwide for its crystal clear water and extensive open caverns, making it a popular destination for recreational diving. The site is accessible only via prior bookings, which can be made online or by phone.

Kilsby Sinkhole is the only site of its kind in Australia that welcomes snorkellers and Open Water certified divers, through to those with Cave or Technical dive training. Snorkellers, Freedivers and Open Water divers must be guided by an approved Dive Instructor. With a depth of almost 30 metres directly from the pontoon, the site is a perfect location for freediving and training camps are regularly held onsite.

item.title: Kosovo
item.description:
About

Kosovo, despite its small size, has a high concentration of karst terrain, especially in the western and southern parts of the country. This has resulted in a dense network of caves, some of which are significant in size, depth, and scientific interest. While dry caving is relatively well developed, cave diving in Kosovo remains largely unexplored—but there is real potential for pioneering dives, particularly in karst springs and resurgences.

item.title: Little Blue Lake - 5L9
item.description:
From CaveDB

Little Blue is a commonly used as a local swimming hole as well as being a popular basic cave diving site. It is relatively easy to access from the road and has a decent equipment assembly table and stairs running straight down to the water. The clarity can be quite poor and it is relatively deep getting down to nearly 40m. You should take care on your air consumption and non deco time as you will run into deco quite quickly. Visibility can be quite poor especially in the top 20m and there is little to see beyond random junk that has been thrown into it over the years. The rubbish include barbed wire and other random items so take care around the bottom not to get snagged. During summer months it can be full of locals swimming and dive bombing from the top so be careful not to get landed on.

item.title: Madagascar
item.description:
About

Why: Massive karst regions like the Tsingy de Bemaraha and Ankarana contain hundreds of limestone caves, many barely explored or surveyed. The warm climate and remoteness suggest the potential for flooded sections, especially during the wet season.
Status: Speleologists have mapped many dry caves, but little to no published cave diving.
Opportunity: First cave dives, exploration of submerged passages during seasonal floods.

item.title: Madura Cave
item.description:
From CaveDB

access track is first left off road from madura road house

small enterence hole to left hand side of depression. large cave with solution tube hole to surface mid way into first chamber.

cave splits into two tunnels with soft sediment on floor getting smaller as you go through. tunnels go for a few hundred meters

ASF has a cave tracker in the left hand side of the tunnel around 150m into cave.

item.title: Moko Morete
item.description:
From CaveDB

Moko Morete opens in a vast blue hole. An underwater passage to the west can be followed 10 to 15 m, but then it becomes too narrow. It may lead to Gua Moko. The main passage begins to the east. With 403 m, it is one of the longest sumps explored on Muna so far. The maximum depth is 21 m. The inner part is huge, ending in a collapse due to the very soft nature of the limestone. The cave still needs to be thoroughly explored. Only the few first meters are exposed to daylight.

item.title: Murra-El-Elevyn - 6N47
item.description:
About

Also known as Cocklebiddy 3 Mile Cave, the entrance is a small overhanging doline 20m in diameter. A 20m pitch leads to a loose talus and silt slope which becomes a boulder floored passage after the doline. The passage continues to a small lake at 89m. There are wetas near the entrance of the cave. There was a thylacine carcase found on early trips to the cave. Uphill of the lake leads to further boulder floored chambers with bats. There are 300m of low maze passages beyond the lake, which contains gypsum flowers and needles. The cave breathes in maze section. Beyond the lake underwater, the cave extends into a series of passages and boulder floored chambers with an average depth of 10m. There is a section of silt floor and parts of the cave passages which have a colouration similar to “coffee and cream”. There are three cave passages which have small air chambers.

item.title: Nettlebed - 5L290
item.description:
From CaveDB

Nettlebed Cave is home to a range of interesting features for cave divers to explore. The wall-scratchings which can seen once inside “The Gallery” are probable evidence of megafauna, while entrenched seashells provide insight into the cave’s Ice Age inhabitants.

Beyond The Gallery, the cave drops deeper and breaks into additional rooms containing many large, dark silt-covered boulders, black walls and white-clay floored passages.

The cave finishes in a chamber at 28m, but with an actual penetration distance from the surface of 80m.

item.title: North Macedonia
item.description:
About

Matka Canyon Caves - Facebook

North Macedonia offers some intriguing caving opportunities, particularly for dry cave exploration, with limited—but potentially promising—cave diving potential. The country lies within the Dinaric karst region, which spans much of the western Balkans and is known for extensive limestone formations, karst plateaus, sinkholes, and underground rivers. Here’s a breakdown of what you can expect:

Dry Caving Opportunities

North Macedonia is home to hundreds of known caves, many of which remain poorly explored. Some of the most significant include:

item.title: Nurina Cave
item.description:
From CaveDB

Situated to the east of Madura Pass, approximately 1400km from Perth, you’ll find a fascinating cave on the Roe Plain. Here, the limestone surface is in close proximity to the water table. This underwater cave is a complex network of intersecting fissures, with a generally small breakdown passage. It features distinct bedding planes at depths of 3, 5, and 7 meters, which house stunning horizontal elliptical phreatic passages as well as low flat passages, all interconnected. The deepest point is a 7m bedding plane, and so far, 410m of underwater passage has been explored (as of February 2004).

item.title: Olwolgin - 6N
item.description:
From CaveDB

Overview

Located in the vast expanse of the Nullarbor desert, over 2500 km from Melbourne, Australia, lies a hidden gem known as the Olwolgin Cave. This underwater cave system, named after a nearby bluff on the Roe Plain escarpment, is a fascinating destination for adventurous divers and explorers.

Getting there

The journey to Olwolgin Cave is an adventure in itself. It begins with meticulous packing for a road trip to the middle of nowhere. The route takes you through major multilane highways, rolling hills, and farmed greenery, before the landscape gives way to the single-lane highway snaking along the southern coastline of the continent.

item.title: Palau
item.description:
About

Best time to go is May (Rubens) Palau offers year-round diving, but the dry season from October to May is considered the best time to visit. During this period, divers can expect calmer seas, better visibility (often exceeding 30 meters), and a higher likelihood of encountering diverse marine life.

Palau’s Rock Islands, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are characterized by uplifted coral limestone formations that have been sculpted over millions of years by natural processes such as erosion, tidal action, and sea-level changes. This has resulted in a stunning karst topography featuring mushroom-shaped islands, caves, sinkholes, and underground channels. These formations are not only geologically significant but also contribute to the rich biodiversity and unique ecosystems found in the region

item.title: Permandian Moko
item.description:
From CaveDB

Alam Moko is a vast blue hole close to 30 m in diameter with direct exposure to daylight, surrounded by cliffs up to 6 m high. One passage develops to the west, but it is too narrow to allow the passage of a diver. The main passage develops to the east. It is in complete darkness, 16.5 m deep and about 65 m long ending in a collapse of stones.

item.title: Photogrammetry
item.description:
Processing

  • Grace Cave
  • LiDAR of Reynella Cave

Ideas

  • Photogrammetry - Rig Setup For a dedicated Windows photogrammetry box:
  • Install NVIDIA Studio Drivers (not Game Ready)
  • Disable Windows sleep/hibernation
  • Set Power Plan to High Performance
  • Exclude project folders from Windows Defender scanning
  • Disable automatic reboots for updates
  • Put your project cache/scratch on a separate NVMe drive

Other

  • Share models on Soggy Wombats Website

Software

  • Metashape
    • Buy Metashape Pro? & run Metashape Cloud?
  • Reality Capture
    • Free it but can’t do spherical/360 images
  • Postshot
  • Polycam phone app

Data Storage & Processing

  • On-Prem: SSD storage in a NAS (see Gear)
    • Citrix to remotely access home server?
  • Portable: Rugged 2Tb HDD - $130
  • Cloud: AWS with S3 bucket
    • ChatGPT - Remote Photogrammetry with StarLink
    • Use S3 to store final models that display on a website - Stack Overflow
    • Amazon Console - Login
    • ChatGPT - Cloud-Based Photogrammetry]]
    • Run Photogrammetry in the Cloud - AWS How-To <– READ THIS IT’S IMPORTANT
  • Other Cloud: MaxCloudOn is dedicated photogrammetry service with $20 credit
  • belowJS - Sharing cave models

Gear

  • X5 - Wired - X5 Review - X5 replacement lenses ($30)
    • Benefit of X5 having user replaceable lens - scratches from dry caving
    • Dive Case Polish? Autosol 75ml Acrylic Polish TESTED - POOR RESULTS
  • Lighting
    • Third BigBlue VL18000PBRC? $1500AUD (Adreno)
    • BigBlue Remote Control - $150US (From BigBlue)
  • Geolocation
    • Insta360 GPS Remote for $80 from AliExpress
    • Drone - use metadata from photos
  • LiDAR
    • Raven Spatial Scanner - $999USD
      • Don’t get RTK - no GPS inside caves, and GPS fix provided by drone)
      • Don’t need Max version - use X4/5 for high res textures

Other Ideas

  • Improved photogrammetry rig?
    • 4x GoPros on helmet? Concerns about weight/neck strain
    • Clamp two Carbon Fibre Floats
      • 4x triple ball clamps
      • 4x GoPros at the front
      • 3-4x lights at the back
    • Hose Clamps with foam/rubber between?)
  • Is there an exploration/business plan here?
    • How do you visit amazing places share the experience?
  • Drones are essential for geolocation
    • Pre-program flight/photography path to centre on a cave, then fly around it in a manner that captures the data required for a 3D model?
    • Insta360 Drone with 360 cameras
  • Marcin Stempniewicz - Maria Concordia Project, running a course on presenting 3D models
    • Youtube - Marcin’s U3DA Course (Demo)
    • Underwater photogrammetry Academy
    • Do a Domestika course on using Blender
  • Collect Photogrammetry data for a caving game?
  • Upload 360 footage to Google Street View Studio
    • Requires GPS data (upload GPX file)
  • Work with ASF to 3D model important caves - become the specialist for photogrammetry here.
    • Important to include radio location - Aren Leishman
      • Place pingers in cave, do photogrammetry scan, then use pinger GPS data to scale the size of the photogrammetry data
      • Place pingers on 1st dive (one at entrance, one at far end), get gps fixes on surface, then do photogrammetry while recovering pingers

Notes from Will Passos

Hey, couple of things to make your life easier if you want to process up to the model…

item.title: Picanninnie Ponds - 5L72 - CLOSED
item.description:
From CaveDB

Piccaninnie Ponds is a karst sinkhole located in the Limestone Coast region of South Australia, approximately 32 kilometres southeast of Mount Gambier. The site is recognized as a wetland of international importance and is listed under the Ramsar Convention. The ponds are renowned for their crystal-clear water, which supports aquatic vegetation up to 15 metres below the surface.

Piccaninnie Ponds is a popular destination for recreational diving, attracting both snorkelers and cave divers. The site contains three main features of interest to cave divers: The First Pond, an open depression about 10 metres deep with a silt floor and much aquatic life; The Chasm, a sinkhole over 100 metres deep; and The Cathedral, a large underwater cavern with majestic white walls of sculptured and scalloped limestone.

item.description:
Portugal is listed under Europe in Cave Regions.

Cave Regions

Caves & Dive Sites

  • See the linked cave regions above.

Backlinks

  • Cave Regions
  • Diving

Existing Notes

Go in September, then stay for Diving Talks Conference

About

  • Algarve coastal sea caves:
    Best between June and September, when visibility is highest and seas are calm. This is when marine traffic is highest too, so early or late in this period is best for quieter exploration.
  • Inland karst systems (e.g., Mira de Aire, Serras de Aire e Candeeiros):
    Access is best in spring and autumn (April–June, September–October) when groundwater levels are manageable and temperatures mild. Winter rains can flood systems, and summer can see restrictions due to fire risk or access limits.
  • Water Temperatures: Range from 14–26°C depending on depth and region, so a 5–7mm wetsuit or drysuit is advised for inland cave systems, even in summer.
  • Local Festivals & Holidays: Avoid major holiday periods (especially August) to reduce crowds and booking difficulties.

item.title: Rwanda
item.description:
HIGH RISK - ALL KNOWN KARST <10KM FROM Democratic Republic of Congo

About

Karst around Bugarama and Nyungwe Forest

  • Why: Karst features in the southwest near the Congo border, with known limestone outcrops.
  • Status: Almost no documented speleology or diving.
  • Potential: Blue holes and flooded sinkholes possibly linked to geothermal springs.
  • Best Season: June to September (Long Dry season)

Why June to September?

  • Dry Conditions:
    Rwanda has two dry seasons — the long dry season (June to September) and a shorter one (December to February). The long dry season offers the most stable weather, lowest rainfall, and easiest overland travel, which is essential when accessing remote or undeveloped cave sites.
  • Reduced Flood Risk:
    In karst systems, dry seasons reduce the chance of sudden flooding, improve visibility, and lower flow rates in submerged passages — critical factors for safe cave diving.
  • Cool but Comfortable Climate:
    Rwanda’s elevation means temperatures are generally mild year-round (20–27°C in the day), but the dry season offers the most reliable surface conditions for expedition logistics.

Important Cave Diving Context for Rwanda

  • Emerging or Untapped Potential:
    Rwanda is not currently a mainstream cave diving destination, but it does have significant volcanic and karst features — especially around the Northwest (Musanze) and Western regions (near Lake Kivu and Nyungwe Forest). Several lava tube caves like Musanze Caves exist, and while most are explored on foot, they may include submerged sections not yet fully mapped.
  • Exploratory Diving:
    Any cave diving in Rwanda is likely to be exploratory in nature, potentially requiring permits, environmental approvals, and collaboration with local authorities or researchers.
  • Access & Logistics:
    Remote locations, lack of existing dive infrastructure, and the potential need for self-supported expeditions (including rebreathers or portable compressors) make timing your trip for the dry season even more important.

Other Considerations

  • Permits & Conservation:
    Rwanda is extremely conservation-focused — engaging with the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) or local geologists would be essential for any diving expedition.
  • Rainy Season (March–May, October–November):
    Avoid these months. Roads may become impassable, visibility drops, and cave flooding becomes a serious risk.

1. Musanze Region (Northern Province)

  • Geological Features: This area is characterized by extensive lava tubes formed from ancient volcanic activity, particularly from the Bisoke and Sabyinyo volcanoes.
  • Notable Caves:
    • Musanze Caves: Approximately 2 km long with 31 known entrances, these caves are part of the lava basaltic layers and are the most frequently visited in Rwanda.
    • Ubuvumo Bwibihonga: The longest cave in Rwanda, featuring a multi-level system of parallel lava tubes.
  • Exploration Potential: While these caves are primarily known for dry exploration, the presence of lava tubes suggests potential for submerged sections, especially during the rainy season when water levels rise. (Visit Rwanda)

2. Nyungwe Forest Region (Western Rwanda)

  • Geological Features: This region is part of the Albertine Rift and is characterized by ancient Precambrian rocks, including quartzite and schist. While traditional karst formations are less common here, the area’s complex geology may host unique subterranean features.
  • Exploration Potential: Limited information is available about caves in this region, suggesting an opportunity for pioneering exploration.

The northwestern and western parts of Rwanda, particularly near the Volcanoes National Park and along the Albertine Rift, contain limestone and dolomitic formations associated with the uplifted sedimentary sequences of the rift system.

Existing Notes

About

Central Highlands Karst

  • Why: Significant limestone in the Central and Northern provinces, including areas near Dambulla.
  • Status: Largely undocumented in terms of cave exploration, but karst water systems are present.
  • Potential: First cave diving in small flooded sinkholes or phreatic systems during wet season.
  • Best Season: January to March (dry season for access).

Pamir-Alay Karst System

  • Why: High-altitude karst with known large caves like Festivalnaya and resurgence-fed systems.
  • Status: Explored by Russian and European dry cavers, but no known cave diving.
  • Potential: Alpine resurgence diving and high-altitude sump exploration in untouched systems.

item.title: Tank Cave - 5L230
item.description:
From CaveDB

Tank cave in Mount Gambia, South Australia is one of Australia’s most popular and largest mapped submerged cave. It has over 7km of passage of which most contain fixed lines. It is located in farmland about 20km outside Mount Gambia and its entrance is on land owned by the Cave Divers Association of Australia. The cave is a complex system of interconnected tunnels that requires complex navigation and even after gaining the needed advance cave standard you need to follow a strict familiarization schedule consisting of 18 dives that progressively expand your experience of the system. Care must be taken with planning and cookie discipline due the complexity of dives and particular care taken not to cut corners and potentially miss an obscured branch of line. A large amount of the cave are accessible to back-mount divers but many sections required side-mount configuration to penetrate. Water temperature is relatively constant 14 Celsius year round and a dry suit with suitable thermal protected is needed. Much of the cave is quite shallow around 10-12 metres with deeper sections as you get to the Fossil Cave side getting to 20+ metres.

item.title: The Shaft - 5L158
item.description:
From CaveDB

The Shaft is a sinkhole located near Mount Gambier in South Australia. It is a popular destination for cave divers, known for its clear water and interesting internal structure.

The Shaft is the site of a tragic scuba diving incident that occurred on May 28, 1973, which claimed the lives of four recreational scuba divers. The incident led to the formation of the Cave Divers Association of Australia and the development of the South Australian Police Underwater Recovery Squad .

item.description:
Timor-Leste is listed under Oceania in Cave Regions.

Cave Regions

Caves & Dive Sites

About

  • Why: Tectonically uplifted limestone karst; similar geology to adjacent parts of Indonesia.
  • Status: Limited cave documentation; no cave diving.
  • Potential: First exploration of resurgence systems and flooded karst valleys.
  • Best Season: May to October. Best month = September

Trips

  • Flights daily Darwin to/from Dili
  • Previous exploration by Portuguese cavers
    • Get Will Passos for Portuguese?

    • Organised by 4 Portugese Caving clubs
    • Bakua Sink (Maubisse, Ainaro), resurgence at Biribui Spring?
  • Lautém Municipality: Lene Hara Cave, Jerimalai, Ile Kére Kére

item.title: Tommy Graham's Cave - 6N56
item.description:
Other Descriptions

About

The entrance to the cave is a large doline 50m in diameter. The obvious route into the doline leads to short cave below the Northwest cliff line.

The main cave has been described as a “wombat- sized hole” which is found in the Southeast end of the doline, about 3m down from the level of the plain. There is a visitor book on a rock shelf in the entrance. The way on is not obvious and goes through a rock squeeze at the end of the low entrance chamber.

item.title: Tonga
item.description:
About

Best time is April to October (Dry season). Excellent visibility and the chance to encounter humpback whales during their migration (June to November).

Tonga’s geological landscape includes islands with uplifted coral limestone formations, leading to the development of karst topography characterized by caves, sinkholes, and underground drainage systems. Notably, ʻEua Island exhibits extensive limestone formations with karst features, including numerous caves formed through the dissolution of carbonate rocks.

item.title: Tunisia
item.description:
About

🪨 Limestone Karst and Caves in Tunisia

Tunisia’s karst topography is primarily found in its central and western regions, characterized by extensive limestone and dolomite formations. These areas host numerous caves formed through karstification processes.(geologyscience.com)

  • Djebel Serj: Located in central Tunisia, this limestone mountain is home to significant cave systems, including the Ain Dhab and Mine caves. The Mine Cave is considered the longest in Tunisia, extending over 4 kilometers. (en.wikipedia.org, en.wikipedia.org)
  • Jebel Bargou: Adjacent to Djebel Serj, this area also features karstic formations with caves developed in Aptian limestone. (en.wikipedia.org)
  • Cave Nefza: Situated in the northwest, this cave extends approximately 310 meters and showcases various speleothems. (en.wikipedia.org)

These karst systems are significant both geologically and hydrologically, contributing to the region’s groundwater resources. (link.springer.com)

item.title: Weebubbie Cave - 6N2
item.description:
From CaveDB

Depth: 40+ metres (130+’) Visibility: 30+ metres (100+’) Water temperature: 17-19°C (63-66°F)

Other Descriptions

About

Description: The entrance to Weebubbie Cave is a large doline 45m in diameter, with a boulder “saddle” at its base. A large main passage with a broken rock floor leads to two lakes at 84m below the surface. The route through the cave is track marked with reflective markers. The cave contains bats and bacterial colonies.
